title: Every Polish group has a non-trivial topological group automorphism

predicted_errors.error_location: Proof of Theorem 1.1, construction of H and extension of φ
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The proof concludes from the fact that every individual t ∈ U \ {0} is linearly independent from {x_i} that one may choose an arbitrary nontrivial automorphism of L = span{x_i} and extend it by fixing every y ∈ Y. This does not follow: Y being linearly independent and each y individually lying outside L does not imply span(Y) ∩ L = {0}. There may be a relation x = y_1 + ... + y_k with nonzero x ∈ L and distinct y_j ∈ Y. Fixing all y_j then forces x to be fixed, whereas an arbitrary chosen nontrivial automorphism of L may move x. Thus the prescribed map need not be well-defined on H at all. The argument would require a proof that L and span(Y) form a direct sum, which is absent and is not implied by the stated properties.

The text states that V' is constructed so that "(x + V') + (y + V') = ∅" for distinct x,y ∈ L, and repeats the same expression in the following displayed justification. With standard set addition, two nonempty sets have nonempty Minkowski sum, so this is impossible: (x+V')+(y+V') contains x+y+v+v' for any v,v' ∈ V'. The subsequent maximality argument actually needs and later uses the intersection statement (x+V') ∩ (y+V') = ∅. The displayed claim and its justification therefore have the wrong operation and must be corrected.

The abstract claims that there are "no uniquely homogeneous Polish groups," and Theorem 3.1 says "A non-trivial Polish group cannot be uniquely homogeneous." Both are false as written. The discrete two-element Polish group Z_2 is uniquely homogeneous as a space: for every ordered pair p,q there is exactly one bijection/homeomorphism sending p to q. Equivalently, its only automorphism is the identity and the two translations supply exactly one homeomorphism between each ordered pair. This is also the exceptional case explicitly excluded by Theorem 1.1 (which assumes more than two elements). A singleton is another counterexample to the abstract's unrestricted wording. The conclusion would need a qualification such as "with more than two elements."

predicted_errors.error_location: Paragraph after Theorem 1.1 concerning extended mapping class groups, citation [4]
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper asserts without any surface-complexity restrictions that for extended mapping class groups of connected metrizable surfaces (and finite-index subgroups), every algebraic automorphism is induced by conjugation, and hence that every extended mapping class group is isomorphic to its automorphism group. This is false for low-complexity surfaces. For example, the extended mapping class group of the unmarked sphere is C_2, whereas Aut(C_2) is trivial, so the group is not isomorphic to its automorphism group. Standard rigidity/automorphism theorems for mapping class groups require substantial hypotheses and do not support the unrestricted assertion attributed to [4].

The document contains numerous numbered citations, including assertions explicitly attributed to [3], [4], [5], and [11], but contains no bibliography or reference list identifying any of [1]–[12]. Consequently the cited results, page references, and attributions cannot be checked. A complete paper must provide the corresponding bibliographic entries.
